brief.head: Not a low-skill game
brief.text: A world-class export plant hires 10,000 workers at 8,000 rupees a month, Ajay Shah said, but also 1,000 capable people, 100 super-capable ones and 20 global geniuses. {#geniuses}

brief.head: Refund the exporter
brief.text: Elsewhere, VAT is fully refunded at the point of export. India’s GST and RoDTEP refund only part, and slowly. Indian exporters carry taxes their rivals don’t, Ajay Shah said. {104-C15}

brief.head: Court as cheap lender
brief.text: Owe 100 rupees, stall ten years in court, then pay at 5 per cent interest, and you have had a cheap loan. Shubho Roy wants punitive court rates. {104-C14}

brief.head: Two passports, please
brief.text: In the UK, Ajay Shah believes, people may hold two passports, so one can be away for a visa while they travel on the other. India makes it hard. {104-C17}

brief.head: Plan the factory town
brief.text: Ajay Shah cited Bimal Patel’s talk at the Emerging Markets Conference: about 40 per cent of urban land should go to streets and parks. Shah wants factories planned in. {104-R21}

thought.who: Ajay Shah, on the fourth way a factory differs from an office

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on India’s missing factories
lead.head: Services sprint, factories stall
body: Indian manufacturing is broken, Ajay Shah declared, and he brought the numbers to prove it. For 30 years its share of GDP has been stuck between 15 and 20 per cent; in the middle stage of development, countries reach 40 to 50 per cent.
Its share of jobs is small and not rising. The export figures are starker still.
Over a decade, services exports grew from $151 billion to $341 billion, a rise of 126 per cent. Goods exports grew from $319 billion to $442 billion, only 38 per cent in nominal dollars.
Allow for American inflation, Shah said, and goods exports grew at “about zero point five percent per year compounded expressed in real USD, which is abysmal”. {104-C01}
The episode, the first of two, grew out of Episode 419 of *The Seen and the Unseen*, Amit Varma’s conversation with Sudhir Sarnobat and Naren Shenoy about the travails of Indian business.
## Why the office won

Why did services take off while factories stalled? Varma’s short answer was that IT services were “relatively new for the Indian state. So it kind of got blindsided by it.” Manufacturing had to carry decades of oppressive regulation. {104-C02}

Shah gave the long answer: eight ways in which a factory differs from an office. A factory is visible, so goons, neighbours and inspectors all come calling. It needs suppliers close by, while services connect over fibre.
It must buy land and machines and carry working capital. It moves goods, not electrons, and pays back over five to seven years rather than one or two.
Above all, it needs what Shah called “a cathedral of complexity”: a web of contracts that courts enforce quickly, so that suppliers deliver on time.
## A history of mistakes
Varma supplied the history. In 1750, he said, India made about 20 to 25 per cent of the world’s manufacturing output, all of it artisanal. By 1900 the share was 2 per cent.
Colonialism took part of the blame, but the bigger cause, he argued, was technological obsolescence: “It just so happens that we got unlucky and industrialised a little later.” {104-S04}

After Independence the state made things worse. Jawaharlal Nehru’s mistakes, import substitution and the belief that competition is wasteful, followed the fashion of the times. What came after 1965 Varma called unforgivable: India knew it was on the wrong track and went deeper. {104-C07}
The 1970s, when cheap labour could have made India a manufacturing superpower, were lost.
## Twelve problems, two governments

Shah then listed twelve problems that hold manufacturing back today: labour law and minimum wages, land, the location of workers, electricity, trade barriers, finance, a state suspicious of the world, hostility to size, slow courts, unrefunded taxes on exports and a shortage of skilled people.
Infrastructure made the list too, but Shah no longer thinks it is the binding constraint.
Five of the twelve, he said, belong to the union government and seven to the states. “Each state is a master of its own destiny on seven out of the twelve things.” {104-C18}
Varma said he would watch the episode “again and again and again”, and might ask their editor for a version without himself in it.
Next week, the hosts promised, they would ask whether a country can have a growth strategy in which manufacturing is not of essence.

second.label: Services v manufacturing
second.head: A factory can’t hide
second.deck: Ajay Shah on why being visible is a liability for India’s factories
body: A factory is big and bulky, and everyone can see it. Ajay Shah borrowed a word for this from James C. Scott’s *Seeing Like a State*: factories are legible.

Once one goes up, local people ask it to fund a puja or build a school. Local goons demand money before its trucks can pass. Every imaginable inspector shows up to extort. Factories, Shah said, are sitting ducks. {104-C03}

A services firm sits on one floor of an innocuous office building, among many firms, with no single concentrated owner. That, Shah said, makes services “a little more hidden, it’s a little genteel”. {#genteel}

quote.text: All the problems of extortion and expropriation by private persons and by state personnel afflict factories more.

second.caption: factories as sitting ducks

third.head: A tale of two Bengals
body: Ajay Shah offered what he called a North Korea-South Korea comparison: “a communist country called West Bengal, where the minimum wage is 13,000 rupees”, and “a capitalist country called East Bengal”, where he thought it was seven or eight thousand. {104-J06}
East Bengal built the amazingly successful garment export industry. In India, Shah said, high minimum wages leave only capital-intensive garment factories viable, in a country with mass poverty.
Amit Varma explained why. If a worker’s labour is worth 8,000 rupees, a 13,000-rupee floor does not raise his pay. It makes his job illegal, and he earns “a big fat zero”. {104-C09}
Shah called it the state using “its monopoly of violence” to stop a voluntary deal between consenting adults.

p2.title: The broken factory
p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s diagnosis and Amit Varma’s history of how India’s state hobbled its factories, chapter by chapter

sections.label: The hard facts
sections.head: Stuck at twenty per cent
sections.caption: the hard numbers
body: Ajay Shah set out to prove that Indian manufacturing is broken, with two qualitative claims and one set of hard numbers.
The first claim: when GDP grows fast, manufacturing’s share should rise a lot. In India it has been stuck between 15 and 20 per cent for 30 years. “20% of GDP ain’t much,” he said.
The second: manufacturing’s share of employment should rise with growth. It has no meaningful presence in overall employment, and it is not going up.
Amit Varma asked what a healthy figure would be. In rich OECD economies the share declines again, Shah said, but there is a middle zone where it goes up to 40 to 50 per cent of GDP.
## The export test
The starkest evidence was in exports. Services exports grew from $151 billion to $341 billion in a decade, a gain of 126 per cent. “That happened to my weight, but continue,” Varma said. {104-J04}
Goods exports grew from $319 billion to $442 billion, 38 per cent in nominal dollars. American inflation in the decade was almost 3 per cent, Shah noted, not the 2 per cent target.
That leaves real growth of about half a per cent a year, “which is abysmal”. {104-C01}
~ “It behoves all of us,” Shah said, “to think about what is wrong and what should be done about it.”

quote.text: There is a serious crisis with manufacturing in India.

sections.label: Factory v office
sections.head: Electrons travel light
sections.caption: why factories differ from offices
body: Ajay Shah counted eight ways in which a manufacturing problem differs from a services problem. The first, that factories are visible and so attract extortion, he called legibility.

The second is linkages. Factories thrive among specialised suppliers close by, but in India something trips up a few of them. “One fellow will go down with a labour law, one fellow will go down with some banks and creditors,” he said. Services connect over fibre-optic cables and do not care where anyone sits. {104-C04}

Then capital: a services firm rents its floor and its computing, while a factory buys land and machines and carries working capital. It needs reliable electricity, it moves goods, and it pays back over five to seven years, not one or two.
## The cathedral

Last come contracts. Global buyers run just-in-time supply. If a supplier fails to deliver 5,000 ball bearings on the day, the assembly line freezes, and a court should promptly impose liquidated damages. Without that, firms hoard inventory or deal only with family. {104-C05}
Nor is this low-skill work, Shah said. It is “a high wire act” of perfect quality, quantity and timing. {104-C06}
~ Amit Varma’s shorter answer was that IT services were new, so no decades of regulation lay in wait for them. Manufacturing inherited it all. {104-C02}

quote.text: to do manufacturing well is to achieve a cathedral of complexity, where there’s a rich array of contracts that surround the process of manufacturing

sections.label: How we got here
sections.head: Forgivable, then unforgivable
sections.caption: the state’s long war on factories
body: India’s fall to 2 per cent of world manufacturing came under the British, Amit Varma said, and owed much to the Industrial Revolution. Independent India made things worse.

Jawaharlal Nehru made two big mistakes. Import substitution cut India off from world trade, and its share fell from about 2 per cent in 1947 to 0.5 per cent by 1990. In the 1960s, Hong Kong’s income from exports was as much as India’s entire income. {#hongkong}

The second was P.C. Mahalanobis’s belief that competition is wasteful: why should two companies make cars? So many existing laws still rest on it, Varma said. “Why should ten people make potato chips?” {104-J17}
## After 1965
Varma finds it hard to blame Nehru, who followed the fashion of the times. But by 1965 the model was visibly failing. He called Indira Gandhi’s economic policies crimes on humanity. {#indira}

The list is long: industrial licensing, the MRTP Act against big firms, small-scale reservations for goods such as garments and shoes, FERA against foreign capital, and the Industrial Disputes Act, under which a firm of 100 workers needed state permission to fire anyone. Firms stayed at 99, or 19, or nine. {104-C08}
~ The 1970s, when cheap labour could have made India a manufacturing superpower, were lost. “We simply never got on that bus,” Varma said.

quote.text: What happened after 1965, frankly, is unforgivable. We knew we were on the wrong track and we deepened our journey into that wrong track.

sections.label: Today, part one
sections.head: Factories belong in cities
sections.caption: what holds factories back today
body: Ajay Shah listed twelve problems that hold Indian manufacturing back today. The first is labour.

Maharashtra, he granted, has reined in wildcat unions. “I will point out that there are many states in India that are not called Maharashtra,” he added. {104-J07} Unions, he said, are a form of market power, which the state should counteract, not enshrine.
Then minimum wages. As Milton Friedman explained, Amit Varma said, a minimum wage does not lift a low-paid worker to the legal floor: it outlaws his job. {104-R08}
Infrastructure has improved a great deal, Shah said, without a matching rise in FDI, manufacturing exports or factory jobs, so it is no longer the binding constraint. {104-R09}
## Where the workers live

Land is the third problem, and where workers will live the fourth. Prices, Shah said, look like a China-style bubble. A village of 150 households has about 750 people, of whom at most 100 would go to one factory. {#village} Factories belong near cities, built into urban planning.
Electricity comes next, then trade barriers: a 10 per cent duty on the yarn for synthetic fabric makes Indian cloth dearer than Bangladesh’s or Vietnam’s. {104-C12}
~ Shah finds the Chinese dormitory model, in which factories build hostels for workers, deeply dissatisfying.

quote.text: So you should get out of the romantic idea that there will be factories near villages.

sections.label: Today, part two
sections.head: Pay up, scale up, fly out
sections.caption: finance, size, courts and taxes
body: Finance is the seventh problem. Big Indian companies routinely squeeze small suppliers on payments, which Ajay Shah calls short-sighted, since big firms have cheaper capital. The answer is not a government invoice portal but a bankruptcy code that empowers operational creditors. Push ten important big companies into bankruptcy, he said, and everyone else will get the message. {104-C13}
The eighth problem is the state’s view of the world. “The entire Indian state is organised as an autarky,” Shah said. A tax officer who finds a foreign bank account suspects hawala. {104-C17}
## Size and the courts

Ninth is size. By Wright’s Law, each doubling of lifetime output lifts productivity by about 20 per cent, and in a factory of 10,000 machines every subtle optimisation pays. India feels good about 2,000-worker plants; low-cost leaders elsewhere employ 10,000 to 100,000. {104-C16}
Tenth come the courts. The hosts’ friend Shubho Roy argues that if courts award only 5 per cent interest after ten years of stalling, the defaulter has won a cheap loan. {104-C14}
Eleventh, exporters should get back all the indirect tax they pay. Twelfth, firms must be able to hire foreign talent easily.
~ Five of the twelve sit with the union government, Shah said, and seven with the states. {104-C18}

quote.text: In a very big factory, if you have ten thousand machines, every subtle optimisation is worth it.

side.boxText: Ajay Shah called Episode 419 of *The Seen and the Unseen*, with Sudhir Sarnobat and Naren Shenoy, one of its best. Four and a half hours long, it does the “expensive, difficult field work” researchers would otherwise have to do. {#fieldwork}

contQuote.text: The labour laws in India, which are ostensibly meant to protect workers, actually hurt workers the more. It’s a classic example of why you should judge a policy not by its intention, but by its outcome.

stories.caption: India’s lost share of world manufacturing
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on India’s manufacturing before 1947
stories.head: From a quarter of the world to 2%
body: In 1750, Amit Varma said, India produced about 20 to 25 per cent of the world’s manufacturing output. There were no machines yet; all of it was artisanal. “We were doing damn well.” {#share1750}
By 1900, the share had fallen to about 2 per cent. Historians tell two stories about why, Varma said, and there is some truth in both.

One account, which Dadabhai Naoroji famously gave in the British Parliament, blames colonialism: cheap machine-made cotton textiles from Manchester poured into India and destroyed its weavers. In that telling, Varma said, the British are completely the villains.

Other historians, including Tirthankar Roy, whom both hosts admire, paint a different picture. The Industrial Revolution had arrived, and artisans could not compete with factories. Machine-spun fabric from England hurt handloom workers in places that were never colonised too.
“So it’s really a shift in technology, technological obsolescence which is making this happen,” Varma said. India was unlucky to industrialise later. {104-S04}

Some industry did come. From the 1850s, some of it aided by British capital, there were textile mills in Bombay and Ahmedabad and jute mills in Bengal, and the Tata Iron and Steel Company was set up in 1907. Manufacturing’s share of output almost doubled, from 3.8 per cent in 1913 to 7.5 per cent at Independence.
~ But out of about 350 million people, only two and a half million worked in manufacturing. {#workers} That was the base the new country inherited.
stories.why: The villain-only story leaves out technological obsolescence, Varma argued. India’s deeper misfortune was to industrialise late, leaving a thin base that the independent state then hobbled further with licences, restrictive laws and import substitution. {104-C07}

stories.start: Narayan Murti, the iconic co-founder of Infosys, told me of his personal experience
stories.end: Long delays in getting equipment was fatal for exporters.
stories.caption: the Infosys import licence
stories.kicker: From Montek Singh Ahluwalia’s memoir, read by Amit Varma
stories.head: Licence granted, drive outdated
body: Amit Varma read an anecdote from Montek Singh Ahluwalia’s memoir *Backstage*, told to Ahluwalia by Infosys’s co-founder Narayana Murthy. {104-S03}
In 1983, Infosys wanted to import a Data General MV 8000 computer with three removable disk drives of 200 MB each. Its people had to make several trips to New Delhi to get the import licence.

By the time the licence came, a new disk drive with a capacity of 300 MB was available, and it was 30 per cent cheaper. Naturally, they wanted the latest model. But the licence named the model number, and several more visits to Delhi were needed to change it.
~ In an area where technology was changing rapidly and timely delivery of export orders was crucial, Ahluwalia wrote, long delays in getting equipment were fatal for exporters.
stories.why: Where technology changes faster than files move, licensing was not only mistaken in principle but unworkable in practice. Under it, Varma said, the state determined every action a private player took. {#licensing}

stories.start: One of the most magical things I've seen is in the Baroda region
stories.end: He said what is great about manufacturing is all these linkages
stories.caption: the pipes of Baroda
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a chemical complex near Baroda
stories.head: Pipe dreams in Baroda
body: In the Baroda region, Ajay Shah has seen an entire chemical industry complex in which several private factories run pipes to one another. He called it one of the most magical things he has seen. {104-S01}

The output of one factory flows down a pipe into the next. A meter records how much has gone across, and the supplier invoices on that basis. No trucks, no handling: “there is no friction at all because it’s flowing on pipes”.
This, Shah said, is what the economist Albert Hirschman called linkages: specialised firms, physically close, buying from and selling to one another.

~ In India such networks are fragile. Imagine friends planning twenty interlinked factories within 10 km of one another near Nashik, Shah said: something trips up five out of the ten, and the linkages never come together. {104-C04}

quote.text: complexity doesn’t work well in India because there are too many buggy components in our Indian landscape

stories.start: Okay so we are doing this recording in rural Maharashtra
stories.end: All this stuff is loaded on the backs of the C and I.
stories.caption: power cuts near Bombay
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the power supply where they recorded
stories.head: Lights out, 70 km from Bombay
body: The hosts recorded this episode in rural Maharashtra, a scant 70 km from Bombay. About ten times a day, Ajay Shah said, the MSEB power tripped. {104-S02}

For a manufacturer, that is a no-go: no factory can have its equipment trip five or ten times a day. So everybody has to get a generator, which bulks up capital costs. And running a factory on diesel, Shah said, is horrendously expensive.

Buying from the grid is no escape. Commercial and industrial users are overcharged so that the state can subsidise farmers who get free or nearly free power, households who get 200 or 500 units free, and people who simply steal it.
~ “All this stuff,” Shah said, “is loaded on the backs of the C and I.” Only Gujarat, he added, works reasonably well. {104-C11}

quote.text: it’s astonishing how 10 times a day the MSEB power trips. Like what is this nonsense?

quiz.q: By how much did India’s goods exports grow each year in real terms over the decade?
quiz.a: About 0.5 per cent a year, which Ajay Shah called abysmal.

quiz.q: What did Infosys need several trips to New Delhi for in 1983?
quiz.a: An import licence for a computer; by then a cheaper, bigger disk drive existed.

quiz.q: Whose idea of legibility did Ajay Shah borrow to explain why factories attract extortion?
quiz.a: James C. Scott’s, from *Seeing Like a State*: visible factories are sitting ducks.

quiz.q: What minimum wage did Ajay Shah give for West Bengal, and who built the garment industry?
quiz.a: 13,000 rupees; East Bengal, with a lower minimum wage, built the export industry.

quiz.q: What does Wright’s Law say about a firm’s lifetime output and its productivity?
quiz.a: Each doubling of lifetime output brings about a 20 per cent gain in productivity.

quiz.q: Of Ajay Shah’s twelve problems, how many are in the hands of the states?
quiz.a: Seven; the union government handles five, so each state shapes its own destiny.
